books.section: Topic 7.4 The Progressives — Taft, Roosevelt, and the Election of 1912
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

stimulus.source_note: Table of 1912 election results; figures from 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9 (rounded).
stimulus.text:
| Candidate | Party | Popular vote | Electoral votes |
| Woodrow Wilson | Democratic | 42% | 435 |
| Theodore Roosevelt | Progressive ('Bull Moose') | 27% | 88 |
| William Howard Taft | Republican | 23% | 8 |
| Eugene V. Debs | Socialist | 6% | 0 |

Percentages rounded. Source: 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9.

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9
stem: According to the table, Wilson won the presidency even though

options.text: he lost the electoral vote to Roosevelt
options.misconception: Wilson won 435 electoral votes, far more than any other candidate.

options.text: he finished second in the popular vote behind Roosevelt
options.misconception: Wilson led the popular vote with 42 percent; Roosevelt was second with 27 percent.

options.text: Taft won the most electoral votes
options.misconception: Taft won only 8 electoral votes, the fewest of the three major candidates.

options.text: he received less than half of the popular vote

rationales.A: Wilson's 435 electoral votes were a landslide. He did not lose the electoral vote.
rationales.B: Wilson led the popular vote at 42 percent. Roosevelt was second at 27 percent.
rationales.C: Taft won 8 electoral votes, the fewest of the three major candidates. He was last, not first.
rationales.D: Wilson's 42 percent was the largest share, but it was less than half. He won because the Republican vote split between Roosevelt and Taft, giving him an electoral landslide on a plurality.
rationales.general:
1. Read Wilson's row. Forty-two percent of the popular vote and 435 electoral votes.
2. Compare the two numbers. A plurality of the popular vote became an electoral landslide.
3. Name the gap. Less than half the people voted for him, yet he won the presidency.
Remember: plurality and majority are different things, so read the percent before deciding how big a win was.
